We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.
2611.29850.comment: 27 pages (13 main + 14 appendix), 9 figures, 20 tables. Project page: https://adonis-galaxy.github.io/Ego2Wrist/

llm.title_ja: Ego2Wrist: エゴセントリックビデオからの手首視点合成のブートストラップ
llm.tldr_ja: Ego2Wristは、約940時間のヘッド・手首カメラのペア記録を用いて、エゴセントリックビデオから同期された手首カメラ視点を合成し、ロボットポリシーの訓練に活用するスケーラブルな手法である。
llm.problem: ロボットマニピュレーションに直接関連する手首カメラの映像を人間の手作業で大規模収集するのは、自然な手の動きを妨げるため困難である。
llm.method: ヘッドカメラと手首カメラのペア動画で学習し、生成された手首視点とヘッド視点の手領域の一貫性を測る手中心クロスビュー一貫性（HCC）を用いて、再帰的な自己改善を行う。
llm.result: 4つのデータセットでの評価において、ファインチューニングされたWorldWanderを上回り、LPIPSを28%削減し、再帰的自己改善により生成品質が段階的に向上した。

2611.29850.tldr_en: Ego2Wrist is introduced, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions and proposes hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view.

2611.29839.title: Dynamics Forcing: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Causal Video World Models
2611.29839.abstract: Causal video world models generate block by block from their own previous outputs. Small errors in early blocks are fed back as history and grow until the scene and the robot fall apart. Teacher forcing trains on clean ground-truth history, so the model never sees the history it will actually condition on, and it also finds a shortcut: copying the previous frame instead of predicting how the scene changes. We present Dynamics Forcing, a training scheme that keeps real video as the only supervision and reshapes how history is presented. History is perturbed in three ways: random noising, self-resampling by the model itself, and joint denoising, in which the most recent blocks are still partly noisy when the next block is predicted. On top of this we move history guidance and first-frame anchor guidance from inference into training, so that the model is pushed to use its history and its reference frame rather than ignore them. Dynamics Forcing needs no teacher model, no distillation, and no additional model at inference. Applied to a 5B video model with LoRA on 77 hours of manipulation video on a single GPU, it better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.

llm.title_ja: Dynamics Forcing: 因果的ビデオ世界モデルにおける誤差蓄積の軽減
llm.tldr_ja: Dynamics Forcingは、履歴データにランダムノイズ付加や自己再サンプリングなどの摂動を加えることで、教師強制の抱えるショートカットを回避し、因果的ビデオ世界モデルにおける誤差蓄積を軽減する訓練スキームである。
llm.problem: 因果的ビデオ世界モデルは過去の出力からブロックごとに生成するため初期の小さな誤差が蓄積して破綻しやすく、従来の教師強制はきれいな正解履歴を使用するためモデルが単なる前フレームのコピーに頼ってしまう。
llm.method: 実ビデオを唯一の監督信号とし、履歴に対してランダムノイズ、モデル自身による自己再サンプリング、最新ブロックの部分的ノイズを残す共同ノイズ除去という3つの摂動を加えて学習させる。
llm.result: 単一のGPU上で77時間のマニピュレーションビデオを用いて5Bのビデオモデルに適用した結果、未見の実世界の後続フレームへの適合性が向上し、誤差蓄積が軽減された。

2611.29839.tldr_en: Dynamics Forcing is presented, a training scheme that keeps real video as the only supervision and reshapes how history is presented and better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.

2611.29818.title: How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change?
2611.29818.abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.
2611.29818.comment: Non-archival version presented at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Continually Self-Improving Robots and the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Robot Memory. Code: https://github.com/nesl/memory-for-home-robots
2611.29818.tldr_en: It is suggested that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.

2611.29813.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head for Tiny Vision-Language-Action Models
2611.29813.abstract: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.
2611.29813.tldr_en: The Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH) is proposed, which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state.

2611.29801.title: Superellipse Function: A Powerful Geometric Tool for the Design and Deformation Modeling of Tendon-Driven Continuum Manipulators With Flexural Patterns Experiencing Tension Loss
2611.29801.abstract: In this article, we feature the Superellipse function as a geometric and versatile tool for effective design and modeling of flexural patterns (FPs) in tendon-driven continuum manipulators (TD-CMs) with discontinuous cross section geometries. We also propose a unique complementary mathematical framework and solution algorithm for modeling the effects of distributed and concentrated friction forces- caused by partially-constrained tendons- on tension loss and deformation behavior of a TD-CM designed using a Superellipse function. Particularly, by employing this geometric function, we establish four intuitive functional mappings relating the manipulator's geometric parameters, kinematics, and deformation behavior. Thanks to the features of these intuitive mappings and Superellipse function, we then introduce the concepts of design space and design curve to facilitate intuitive design of a TD-CM with a generic FP geometry experiencing tendon tension loss. To thoroughly evaluate the performance of this novel framework and its aforementioned features, we performed various simulation and experimental studies on TD-CMs designed and fabricated based on a Superellipse function. Results were then analyzed and compared using different error metrics.

2611.29800.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
2611.29800.abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
2611.29800.comment: Manuscript submitted to IEEE OJ-ITS and is currently under review
2611.29800.tldr_en: Fine-tuning on safety-critical scenarios lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.

2611.29771.title: Into My Arms: Structured reinforcement learning for autonomous transport of objects and humans
2611.29771.abstract: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms
2611.29771.tldr_en: The first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution is shown, to the knowledge, with no human intervention during execution.

2611.29749.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
2611.29749.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
2611.29749.tldr_en: CarlHOI is proposed, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies.

2611.29748.title: Performance Evaluation of Nonlinear Model Predictive and Sliding Mode Controllers on a 4-Cable Spatial CSPR in Simscape
2611.29748.abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR) actuated by four cables. The robot is modeled in two parallel ways: (i) via an analytical dynamic model with included cable elasticity and frictional losses, and (ii) in MATLAB Simscape Multibody, capturing realistic physical effects. Both controllers are implemented under identical reference trajectories, system constraints, and tuning strategies. Our results show that NMPC achieves superior tracking accuracy and stronger disturbance rejection compared to SMC, but at the cost of higher computational demand. Moreover, both controllers were tested on an analytical model of the robot and a Simscape model. The close agreement between the two, for both control schemes, confirms the accuracy of the analytical formulation and its consistency with the physics-based simulation. The study highlights the value of physics-based simulation as a complementary tool for validating advanced controllers under realistic conditions, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.
2611.29748.comment: 7 pages, 13 figures, 2 tables. Prepared for the 13th RSI International Conference on Robotics and Mechatronics (ICRoM 2025), Tehran, Iran
2611.29748.tldr_en: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot actuated by four cables, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.

2611.29682.title: SparQ4D: Learning to Act through Sparse 4D Queries
2611.29682.abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces SparQ4D, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, SparQ4D achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
2611.29682.tldr_en: \method is introduced, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates, and is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy.

2611.29681.title: Towards Global Counterfactual-Based Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks
2611.29681.abstract: Graph Counterfactual Explanations (GCEs) have emerged as an effective approach for interpreting Graph Neural Network (GNN) predictions by identifying minimal graph modifications needed to change predictions. However, existing methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) They rely on a post-hoc explanation paradigm, where a separate explainer is trained after the GNN. This sequential optimization prevents the explainer from leveraging how the GNN learned its representations, often resulting in lower-quality explanations. (2) They are largely local, generating counterfactual explanations only for individual samples. Consequently, they fail to capture generalizable patterns across the data distribution, a crucial gap for applications like drug discovery, where global principles enable systematic decision-making across thousands of cases. To address these limitations, we propose GCSGNN (Global Counterfactual-based Self-explainable GNN), a unified framework that integrates counterfactual generation into the GNN architecture, encouraging explanations that faithfully reflect the model's decision-making process. Beyond local explanations, GCSGNN discovers shared latent patterns influencing predictions across graphs, yielding global (i.e., model-level) counterfactual explanations. We further introduce an efficient latent-space counterfactual mechanism that avoids the combinatorial complexity of discrete graph manipulation, enabling scalable discovery of generalizable modification patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GCSGNN outperforms existing methods in generating effective counterfactual explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/gcsgnn.
2611.29681.tldr_en: GCSGNN (Global Counterfactual-based Self-explainable GNN), a unified framework that integrates counterfactual generation into the GNN architecture, encouraging explanations that faithfully reflect the model's decision-making process, is proposed.

2611.29662.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
2611.29662.abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
2611.29662.comment: Under review. Project page: https://grounded-in-contact.github.io/. The second and third authors contributed equally
2611.29662.tldr_en: On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.

2611.29646.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
2611.29646.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_0,π_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $π_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
2611.29646.tldr_en: JKO-GRPO is proposed, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, and extends this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching, to select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.

2611.29637.title: TASC: Time-to-Collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd Attention for Non-Holonomic Service Robots
2611.29637.abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
2611.29637.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication at the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII)
2611.29637.tldr_en: TASC is presented, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy that adds a closing-speed time-to-collision feature.

2611.29627.title: Attacking Tabular Foundation Models: An Experimental Taxonomy of Context Poisoning and Test-Time Evasion
2611.29627.abstract: Tabular foundation models condition predictions on labeled examples supplied at inference time, creating an attack surface that differs from conventional model training. We study four manipulation families (label flipping, backdoor context poisoning, clean-label context selection, and test-time evasion) and organize them by attack stage, label consistency, and distributional realism. TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and XGBoost are evaluated on CIC-IDS2017 and N-BaIoT using a common preprocessing and evaluation pipeline. Backdoor context poisoning provides strong targeted control over the in-context models with little change in clean accuracy, whereas selecting real, correctly labeled boundary-crowding rows causes no systematic accuracy degradation up to a 20% bias fraction. A simplified surrogate-transfer constrained PGD attack inspired by, but not equivalent to, CAPGD also produces test-time evasion, outperforming equal-budget random noise in most settings. The comparison shows that attack effectiveness depends strongly on both where manipulation occurs and how much freedom the attacker has to alter the data.
2611.29627.tldr_en: A simplified surrogate-transfer constrained PGD attack inspired by, but not equivalent to, CAPGD also produces test-time evasion, outperforming equal-budget random noise in most settings.

2611.29610.title: Dr. Grasp-RL: Diverse and Robust Dexterous Grasping via Reinforcement Learning
2611.29610.abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.
2611.29610.tldr_en: A time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control is introduced.

2611.29609.title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding
2611.29609.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
2611.29609.tldr_en: JEPA-Shield is presented, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement and establishes probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning.

2611.29558.title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation
2611.29558.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.
2611.29558.tldr_en: AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time, is introduced and it is shown that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration.

2611.29553.title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
2611.29553.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
2611.29553.comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop "Do Robots Need World Models?". OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=oIzsAcOuYl
2611.29553.tldr_en: In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points and helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks.

2611.29548.title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning
2611.29548.abstract: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.
2611.29548.tldr_en: This work presents Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots, and introduces a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding.

2611.29525.title: Feedback Completion Certificates for Repeated Dwell Tasks with Time Windows
2611.29525.abstract: An inspection robot may owe several measurements at the same station, each with a different window in which a dwell can begin. We ask what a feedback controller must retain about earlier visits to guarantee all remaining deadlines under bounded disturbances. For a common spatial predicate and dwell length, removing redundant windows orders the remaining obligations by both endpoints. On every history without an expired obligation, the served windows form a suffix. One boundary and one capped run length therefore preserve the future satisfaction of the original task. On a verified library of branching motion primitives we use this state to recover a feedback policy. For one task type a scalar threshold per run length suffices, with work linear in the number of listed branches per time layer for fixed dwell. Multiple types require a joint recursion. On a quadrotor inspection library the threshold sweep reduced the cost of constructing a reusable full-domain policy, while a sparse Boolean baseline answered a single initial query faster. In a two-station MuJoCo patrol, three task-aware filters all met every window in twelve paired runs each. Of eight initially certified runs, the completion filter retained the certificate in all eight, compared with three for safety-only filtering.
2611.29525.comment: 37 pages, including appendices with full proofs and experimental details
2611.29525.tldr_en: This work asks what a feedback controller must retain about earlier visits to guarantee all remaining deadlines under bounded disturbances to guarantee all remaining deadlines under bounded disturbances.

2611.29518.title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
2611.29518.abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.
2611.29518.comment: NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. 32 pages, 13 figures. Code and run records: https://github.com/kevinxqiu/reset-dependence
2611.29518.tldr_en: Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols, as well as choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols.

2611.29507.title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
2611.29507.abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.
2611.29507.comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, Submitted to and under review in "International Journal of Intelligent Systems" of Wiley
2611.29507.tldr_en: A Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.

2611.29501.title: MAWAM: Joint Imagination for Collaborative Robot Manipulation with a Multi-Agent World Action Model
2611.29501.abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
2611.29501.tldr_en: MAWAM is presented, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation and develops MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages.

2611.29483.title: Representation Alignment Is Only as Good as the Teacher's Behavioral Structure
2611.29483.abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $π_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $π_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.
2611.29483.comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables, including supplementary material
2611.29483.tldr_en: The behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task, is proposed and introduced, suggesting that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.

2611.29454.title: MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation
2611.29454.abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.
2611.29454.comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Under review at IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
2611.29454.tldr_en: A lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles.

2611.29453.title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
2611.29453.abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
2611.29453.tldr_en: Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa, and OGBench, sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.

2611.29426.title: Phase-Conditioned Action Contracts for Auditable Microsurgical Control
2611.29426.abstract: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,μ\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
2611.29426.tldr_en: A phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation is proposed and the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control is shown.

2611.29421.title: A colour-marker tracker for pose estimation of slender surgical instruments: vision-language-model-guided adaptive colour calibration
2611.29421.abstract: Slender surgical instruments need small, narrow markers for camera-based pose estimation. A colour-stripe marker fits this requirement, but its colours in the image drift from the design values with lighting, printing and camera settings. Because the colours can only be corrected after the marker has been found, methods that rely on the design colours face a circular problem. We propose vision-language-model (VLM)-based adaptive colour calibration and compare it with two rule-based methods, which re-measure the colours from detections made with the design colours: Initial colour update does so once after tracking starts, and Colour adaptation continuously during tracking. VLM guidance uses a fine-tuned VLM to find the markers without relying on the design colours and builds the colour profile from their pixels. Recall/F1 (%) for Initial colour update, Colour adaptation and VLM guidance were 92.0/95.7, 87.8/93.3 and 98.2/99.1 on 672 synthetic image pairs; 51.3/67.2, 48.8/65.0 and 83.8/87.0 on eight degraded laboratory videos; and 38.9/55.2, 19.7/29.7 and 100/100 on a surgical-robot (da Vinci) video with strongly shifted colours. In that video the rule-based methods never found the purple/cyan marker, whereas VLM guidance found all 234 markers with no false positives. In a simulation, the hue boundary between the two stripes moved by less than 0.1 pixel for exposure gains of 0.5-2.0, compared with 2.9-4.0 pixels for a boundary found with a fixed brightness threshold. When the degradation is mild, the rule-based methods, which need no training and no GPU, are sufficient. When the colours change greatly, the gain comes from a VLM-guided candidate search that does not rely on the design colours. Combining colour-stripe markers with adaptive colour calibration enables tracking of slender surgical instruments with small markers.
2611.29421.comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Extended version of a manuscript submitted to a journal
2611.29421.tldr_en: This work proposes vision-language-model (VLM)-based adaptive colour calibration and compares it with two rule-based methods, which re-measure the colours from detections made with the design colours: Initial colour update does so once after tracking starts, and Colour adaptation continuously during tracking.

2611.29383.title: Self-Refining VLA Sampling
2611.29383.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves iteratively updating random noise, and distinct noise samples from the same state can result in distinct trajectories and task outcomes. Existing test-time scaling methods improve action chunk generation via selection, aggregation, or correction, but commonly require the generation of large ensembles of candidates or the training of an external corrector. We adapt Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, to the robotics domain. We find that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data. Across 400 episodes of LIBERO evaluated using SmolVLA, P&P improves upon the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points. Further, episode-level P\&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure (AUC 0.851).
2611.29383.comment: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Learn@Deploy Workshop
2611.29383.tldr_en: P&P, a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, is adapted to the robotics domain and finds that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data.

2611.29377.title: Contact Harness: Enabling VLM Agents to Perform Contact-Rich Manipulation
2611.29377.abstract: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force and tactile feedback provide complementary information, but their semantic ambiguity makes them difficult for agents to use directly. These signals must be interpreted according to their physical meaning, together with task phase and visual evidence. We propose Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions. A compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback. The framework requires no model fine-tuning, task demonstrations, or simulation training. We conduct zero-shot real-robot evaluations using GPT-6 Astra on Rokae and Franka robots. With a single prompt skill, Contact Harness achieves a full-insertion rate of 90.7% across 15 connector types, with further evaluations on a real PC under variations in lighting, background, and position. Across four additional contact-rich tasks, including whiteboard wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting, Contact Harness achieves an average success rate of 100%. On six simulated tasks, Contact Harness reaches 96.7% success, compared with at most 68.3% for pretrained VLA baselines fine-tuned on task demonstrations, showing the potential of agent-based manipulation for contact-rich real-world deployment.
2611.29377.tldr_en: This work proposes Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions, and a compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback.

2611.29369.title: ClothCast: Generative Cloth World Modeling under Partial Observability
2611.29369.abstract: World models support robotic manipulation by predicting how the scene evolves under a planned action. For garments this prediction is notoriously difficult: deformations are complex, and self-occlusion leaves much of the cloth unobserved. Planned gripper trajectories provide a useful motion prior because cloth held by a gripper moves with it, while the remaining deformation must be predicted. We introduce ClothCast, a world model that applies this prior to the cloth's points and learns the residual motion. ClothCast takes one RGB-D observation, the camera pose, the robot's own model and the planned gripper trajectories, with no cloth mesh or material parameters. It lifts the observation to a layered point set that includes hypothesized occluded layers, carries the points with a blended rigid prior derived from the gripper poses, and predicts the residual motion with a video-diffusion point-flow model. Over entire 4- to 11-second episodes at 10 Hz, the moved points are rendered into depth, from which a geometry-conditioned completion model synthesizes RGB; after release, a hand-designed settling step replaces the learned motion. We further release ClothCastBench, 10,000 simulated dual-arm cloth-manipulation episodes with the ground-truth cloth mesh, including occluded layers, at every frame. On 492 held-out episodes, ClothCast achieves 2.5x lower sequence-averaged visible-surface Chamfer distance than Flex-π, the strongest baseline in geometry (14.0 mm vs. 35.6 mm), and 3.7 dB higher cloth-region PSNR than Cosmos-Predict2.5, the strongest baseline in cloth PSNR. On a 50-episode ablation subset, the rigid prior alone, applied to ClothCast's learned initial geometry with the same post-processing, already outperforms both geometry-capable baselines, and the learned residual lowers its error by about a third.
2611.29369.tldr_en: ClothCast is introduced, a world model that applies a rigid prior to the cloth's points and learns the residual motion, and already outperforms both geometry-capable baselines and the learned residual lowers its error by about a third.

2611.29366.title: Scenario Compliant Indoor Pedestrian Trajectory Reconstruction from Partial Observation
2611.29366.abstract: Pedestrian trajectory reconstruction is vital for applications ranging from security surveillance to indoor navigation. While existing probabilistic and generative frameworks have shown success in outdoor GPS-based trajectory imputation, they often fail in indoor settings where movement is strictly governed by dense geometric constraints such as walls and corridors. Standard models typically treat trajectories as unconstrained coordinate sequences, leading to physically infeasible paths with high collision rates. To address this, we propose a map-conditioned generative framework based on conditional diffusion models. Our approach explicitly integrates dense scenario maps as structured spatial inputs via a CNN-based encoder, allowing environmental geometry to guide the iterative denoising process. Furthermore, we employ an endpoint-aware mechanism by embedding observations (start and end points) directly into the scenario map, providing critical spatial anchors through image-level features. Experiments on simulated indoor trajectories and the real-world Shopper trajectory dataset, with three training seeds, show that our method achieves the lowest errors among the compared generative methods. Scene conditioning reduces the collision and invalid rates by 19\% and 46\% on the simulated dataset, whereas on real shopper data the gains are consistent but small, mainly because the model rarely learns to route around obstacles between the endpoints. Compared with a shortest-path planner, which never collides, our method better captures the variability of real motion (31\% lower CRPS), but the timing of stops is reconstructed only partially. These results show that explicit environmental context improves physical consistency, while reconstructing realistic human motion in real indoor spaces remains challenging. Our code is available at https://github.com/dang-qi/trajectory_reconstruction
2611.29366.tldr_en: A map-conditioned generative framework based on conditional diffusion models that explicitly integrates dense scenario maps as structured spatial inputs via a CNN-based encoder, allowing environmental geometry to guide the iterative denoising process.

2611.29346.title: Specification-Aware Sparse Differentiation: Planning under Signal Temporal Logic with Sparsemax Robustness
2611.29346.abstract: Gradient-based optimal control under a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification involves solving a nonlinear program whose constraints are smoothed robustness functions of the trajectory, and automatic differentiation without knowledge of sparsity computes the Jacobian and the Hessian that its solver needs in full. This often renders the problem computationally intractable. The dynamics and the specification prescribe a sparsity pattern through the STL syntax, the windows of the temporal operators and the variables that the predicates read. Standard tools such as CasADi recover this pattern by structural detection. In this work, we propose a method to prescribe such a pattern directly from the task specification. We show that our method allows us to exploit SparseMax, a recently proposed smooth robustness operator that is certifiably sparse and sound. Its derivative is exactly zero at every operand at or below a data-dependent threshold, which structural detection cannot see. We derive the patterns that expose this trajectory-dependent sparsity to sparse automatic differentiation, with a margin test for their reuse and Hessians confined to the variables of each constraint's support. We demonstrate the method on a dual-arm coordination task in which two arms share a hand-off zone divided into cells and one until constraint per scheduled visit keeps the other arm out of a cell until the visitor has left it. The two scenes are a zone of five cells and a circle of 64 cells, with single solves and closed-loop re-planning on a rigid-body simulation. Our exact-Hessian interior-point solves are up to 27 times faster than those with the sound log-sum-exp robustness in CasADi and IPOPT.
2611.29346.tldr_en: A method to prescribe a sparsity pattern directly from the task specification and derive the patterns that expose this trajectory-dependent sparsity to sparse automatic differentiation, with a margin test for their reuse and Hessians confined to the variables of each constraint's support.

2611.29339.title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
2611.29339.abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.
2611.29339.tldr_en: It is argued that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal, and proposed Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about.

2611.29338.title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
2611.29338.abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.
2611.29338.hf_summary_en: nanoAstra combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning to train vision-language models for generalizable robot manipulation, achieving strong zero-shot success and faster streaming execution.
2611.29338.tldr_en: N nanoAstra is introduced, an approach to training vision-language models for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT) and represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions.

2611.29333.title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
2611.29333.abstract: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).
2611.29333.tldr_en: This paper proposes EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft that connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction.

2611.29294.title: RSLaA: Self-Reconfiguring Roadside LiDARs as Agents for 3D Traffic Perception
2611.29294.abstract: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because infrastructure deployment is costly, existing work optimizes RSL configurations once, against road geometry and aggregated traffic statistics, and treats them as fixed thereafter. Traffic flow, however, is inherently dynamic, and a placement optimal on average can be far from optimal at any given moment. We introduce RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows. Since ground truth is unavailable at decision time, the framework centers on surrogate metrics computed solely from a probabilistic occupancy grid of historical observations, which predicts the next-window perception performance of candidate poses. We construct a co-simulation benchmark pairing five candidate surrogates with detector-agnostic ground-truth perception labels at every decision window, identifying the multi-view coverage metric J_mv as the most reliable predictor. Upon this validated surrogate we build two adaptive configuration methods, a receding-horizon (MPC) optimizer and a lightweight MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with centralized training and decentralized execution. Across 10 sites and 89 six-hour traffic scenarios (890 evaluation runs), adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment. Our results indicate that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.
2611.29294.tldr_en: This work introduces RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows, and indicates that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.

2611.29279.title: A2I-VLA: A Two-Stage Vision-Language-Action model with Semantic-Physical Alignment and Integration
2611.29279.abstract: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.
2611.29279.tldr_en: The proposed A2I-VLA is a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model to guide action generation.

2611.29277.title: $ζ_0$: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
2611.29277.abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $ζ_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $ζ_0$ built on $Ψ_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/
2611.29277.comment: 18 pages (including appendix), 10 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/ ; Code & Data: https://github.com/chenyizhi123/Zeta0
2611.29277.tldr_en: zeta_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation, is presented.

2611.29275.title: DriveOddsBench: Are Driving Video World Models Aligned with Real-World Odds?
2611.29275.abstract: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the real outcome among them is uniform in every history, so pooled ranks test them without probability labels. Second, one validated instrument reads the same quantities, such as the lead-vehicle gap and the ego motion, from the generated futures and from the real future, which first passes through the world model's autoencoder so that both are read alike. Third, all confirmatory analyses were frozen before any test clip was measured. We test eleven general and driving world models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories in five scenario families, with 35,200 generated futures. None is aligned, and every model underestimates its uncertainty. The real outcome falls outside the range of all 16 samples in 28-61% of cases instead of the 11.8% expected under the real distribution. Five models are significantly skewed, in opposite directions, and the largest errors are in the ego motion. Nine models beat climatology without being aligned, and among these models neither type nor scale predicts which comes closest.
2611.29275.comment: 22 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/DriveOddsBench-page/ Code: https://github.com/hhjj233/DriveOddsBench
2611.29275.tldr_en: This work test eleven general and driving world models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories in five scenario families, with 35,200 generated futures, finding that none is aligned, and every model underestimates its uncertainty.

2611.29268.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
2611.29268.abstract: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions.
